catalog_quote: Another East Mongolian language, Buriat, provides a second example of a rightmost heavy else leftmost pattern with quantity-sensitive nonfinality. The following data are from the same study as that outlined for Khalkha. Findings are consistent with the description of Buriat given by Poppe (1960: 19) and again clarify the interpretation of ‘penultimate’ heavy syllable. Like Khalkha, primary stress falls on the last syllable if it is the only heavy in the word, otherwise on the rightmost nonfinal heavy, otherwise on the initial syllable. Secondary stress falls on heavy syllables and (possibly) the initial syllable when they do not receive primary stress. audit.recode_to: Provisional, pending Budaev 1981 / Poppe 1960:19: mark 'contested'; likely target is weight-insensitive fixed prominence (dynamic initial + final-syllable pitch rise, long vowels not stress-attracting) per Poppe 1938 sec.53, Bertagaev 1968:16, Budaev 1981 apud Badagarov 2017 — rather than 'weight: rightmost nonfinal CVV else initial'.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: verbatim at the stated place in the held Walker 1997 text (pp.27-28). (2) Deciding source: an unpublished 1997 OT typology manuscript; for Buriat it is second-hand (Poppe 1960:19, not held) plus data 'from the same study' whose only documented recording is of one Khalkha speaker reading Khalkha forms — no Buriat speaker is described anywhere in the ms. Not the best available: Glottolog lists a 340-pp Academy grammar (1962) and Poppe 1960; the Russian literature has a dedicated stress monograph (Budaev 1981) and an experimental study (Bitkeev 1995). (3) Evidence already on file cuts against the coding: Poppe 1938 sec.53 (held, read) = expiratory stress always on the first syllable regardless of vowel length, pitch rise on the final syllable, long non-initial vowels merely sound stronger; Bertagaev 1968:16 (held scanned, decoded) = weak stress tending to a non-initial syllable
audit.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK — agree: lines 1431-1451 (footer p.27) carry the record's passage verbatim ('Another East Mongolian language, Buriat... rightmost nonfinal heavy, otherwise on the initial syllable. Secondary stress falls on heavy syllables and (possibly) the initial syllable'), ex.(33) continues to p.28 (lines 1454-1500) and the 'Khalkha and Buriat words... L H H L' distributivity note is at lines 1516-1526, matching loc. Provenance caveat also verified: fn.5 (lines 1275-1280) documents only 'recordings... of the Khalkha forms as read by a native speaker of Khalkha Mongol

sources.citation: Badagarov, Zhargal B. 2017. O tipakh slovesnogo udareniya v mongol'skikh yazykakh [Word-stress patterns in Mongolic languages]. Vestnik Kalmytskogo instituta gumanitarnykh issledovanij RAN 34(6): 111-116. DOI 10.22162/2075-7794-2017-34-6-111-116.
sources.quote: Distinguishes a Khalkha type (pitch accent shifts onto the first long vowel) from a 'Buryat-Oirat type' characterised by 'a constant position of the accent on the last syllable', tonal/musical in nature [Budaev 1981: 97, 104, 108]; long vowels do not pull the pitch rise onto themselves and an unaccented long vowel becomes overlong, e.g. bur. хаагаа [хаааˈгаа], ооһороо [оооһъˈроо]; Khori Buryat (standard base) is 'close to Kalmyk' in accent, Zakamensk Buryat close to Khalkha. Also reports Bitkeev 1995:83 (experimental, Kalmyk and Buryat): main 'qualitative' stress = clear first-syllable vowel,
sources.note: Open-access synthesis by a Buryat State University Mongolist placing Khori Buryat in a 'final tonal accent, long vowels do not attract' type and summarising Budaev 1981 and Bitkeev 1995; fetched sources now, directly contradicts the record.

sources.citation: Yamakoshi, Yasuhiro. 2011. Shinekhen Buryat. In Y. Yamakoshi (ed.), Grammatical Sketches from the Field, 137-177. Tokyo: ILCAA, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies.
sources.quote: 'Shinekhen Buryat has two accent systems: pitch accent and stress accent. Both systems are phonologically indistinctive, and clitics are not accentuated. a. Stress accent: The initial syllable is stressed. If VV (long vowel or diphthong) are found in other syllables, the syllable that has VV is stressed. E.g. xorgan "lamb", temeen "camel", gasjoon "bitter". b. Pitch accent: VN of the last syllable are pitched higher.' No rule for words with several VV. Variety is Shinekhen (Khori/Aga emigrant Buryat in China; Glottolog lists China Buriat as a separate languoid).
